name: Anabolic diet / high calorie eating

lead: The Anabolic Diet is a cyclic ketogenic plan described in a 1995 book by powerlifter and writer Mauro Di Pasquale, nicknamed the Pork Chop Diet. People use it, along with other heavy-eating approaches, to eat enough to support training and gain muscle size.

It works by alternating low-carbohydrate stretches with higher-carbohydrate periods while keeping calories high, so training is fueled and mass can be added. No studies of its effect on appearance were found, and sources specific to it are limited.

paras: People follow it as a repeating weekly pattern of low-carb eating followed by higher-carb eating, alongside heavy lifting. It is usually run as a bulking phase, and size changes show up over weeks to months of consistent training and eating.

No clinical studies of the diet were found, and the sources reviewed document no risks specific to it. Like other very low-carb and very high-calorie plans, it can be hard to sustain and may not suit people with medical conditions or those on medication; a clinician can advise.

angle.text: The Anabolic Diet is a cyclic low-carb, high-calorie bodybuilding plan used to fuel hard training and push muscle gain. The route to a bigger look runs through eating enough to support training and add mass. No studies of its appearance results were found.

lead: The Anabolic Diet is a cyclic ketogenic diet (CKD) described in Mauro Di Pasquale's 1995 book of the same name, nicknamed the Pork Chop Diet.[1] It is used by lifters who want to add muscle while staying lean, so the physique looks fuller without excess fat. Heavy or high-calorie eating more broadly means eating a calorie surplus to gain weight and muscle, known in bodybuilding as bulking.[2]

Di Pasquale, born in 1945, is an Italian-born Canadian powerlifter, author and low-carbohydrate advocate who won the IPF World Powerlifting Championships in 1976 and the World Games in 1981.[1] He later wrote The Metabolic Diet (2000) and worked as a drug-testing official in professional wrestling.[1]

Wikipedia describes a calorie surplus as the basis of bulking, with larger or longer surpluses adding more body fat, and clean bulks usually using moderate carbohydrate, moderate protein and low fat.[2] No study was found testing the Anabolic Diet for appearance outcomes.

paras: Di Pasquale advocates low-carbohydrate diets and wrote for the bodybuilding press; his books include Drug Use and Detection in Amateur Sports (1984), The Anabolic Diet (1995), Amino Acids and Proteins for the Athlete (1997) and The Metabolic Diet (2000).[1] He worked on writing, research and product development for supplement company EAS from 1997 to 1999.[1]

Wikipedia's bodybuilding article describes bulking as eating in a calorie surplus to build muscle, with the surplus size set by goals.[2] Clean bulking aims to add muscle with little fat and often alternates higher and lower calorie days, while dirty bulking involves a large surplus with little tracking and typically adds significant fat, needing a harder cut afterward.[2] Protein recommendations of 25 to 30 percent of calories are suggested but debated, and some bodybuilders eat five to seven meals a day to manage large food volumes.[2]

A content analysis of the 2009 issues of Men's Health found frequent advice to raise calorie intake (183 references) and protein intake (262 references) to augment muscle mass, described by the authors as an anabolic diet and framed within a mesomorphic body ideal.[3] On T Nation, members describe high-protein, high-fat eating and jokingly call steak and eggs the most anabolic diet.[4][5]

No studies found on the Anabolic Diet for appearance or muscle outcomes. A 1992 randomized trial gave 40 hyperlipidemic patients a high-fat, high-cholesterol diet it labelled anabolic, with or without pyruvate, and measured blood lipids and heart-rate parameters rather than muscle.[6]

lore.intro: On T Nation, the anabolic label is used loosely for high-protein, higher-fat or surplus eating.[4][5]
